title: the oldest labor law
hookLine: the oldest labor law; a day the world can't have

cards: A phone on a Saturday looks like a phone on a Tuesday. Work email. The group chat.
A sale that ends tonight. The world never really closes anymore. Now take a family that, every week, from Friday sunset until the stars come out on Saturday, lets none of that in.
No office. No shopping. In some homes, not even a light switch.
Not a holiday, not a sick day. Just the seventh day, arriving on schedule. Some people call it the oldest labor law there is.

teach.b: Shabbat comes from a Hebrew root, shin, bet, tav, that means to stop. To cease. Not first to relax, or to worship: to stop.
At the end of the creation story, even God stops, and the verb there comes from the same root. English borrowed the word as Sabbath. Then the rabbis asked a practical question: what counts as work?
They listed thirty-nine kinds: planting, baking, writing, building, lighting a fire, and more, drawn from the work it took to build the tent for God in the desert.
So work, on Shabbat, means making and changing things, not how tired you get. Now the part that earns the nickname. The rest day is commanded twice, and the second time it gives a different reason.
You were slaves, so rest, "that thy man-servant and thy maid-servant may rest as well as thou." As well as you. Not after you.

And the list of who rests keeps going: your children, the stranger in your town, even the ox and the donkey. A weekly day off, owed to everyone, written into an ancient law. Jews keep the day in different ways.
Orthodox Jews keep the thirty-nine categories carefully: no driving, no cooking, no phones.
Conservative, Reform and other Jews keep Shabbat in their own ways, through the candles, the meal, synagogue and a slower day, with each community drawing its own lines.
The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel described Shabbat as a palace built in time rather than in space.
You don't travel to it. It arrives, every week, wherever you are.

how: Jews mark Shabbat from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall with candles, blessings over wine and bread, a family meal and synagogue; observant Jews refrain from the thirty-nine categories of work, while others keep it through the meal, rest and a slower day.

games.q: what's inside the day — tap the pairs.

s: Shabbat runs Saturday morning to Saturday night
it runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. a day starts in the evening.
the commandment gives rest to the animals too
the ox and the donkey rest with the household.
every Jew keeps Shabbat the same way
Orthodox Jews keep the thirty-nine categories; others keep it through candles, a meal and rest.

games.q: the second time the rest day is commanded, what reason is given for the servants' rest?
o: because you were slaves in Egypt.
games.why: Egypt: you were slaves once, so your servants rest "as well as thou."

practice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Put one thing down with each breath. The thing you're working on.
The thing you're worried about. The phone, if it's in your hand. For these few breaths, nothing is being made or fixed.
That's the whole idea of Shabbat, very small.

wordCard.voice: Shabbat. To stop: the seventh day, Friday sunset to Saturday stars, a rest owed to everyone in the house. Eleventh word.

orig.note: Hebrew: from the root sh-b-t, to stop or cease. English Sabbath comes from it.

carryVoice: Your line: stop. it's already Friday. Rest isn't a prize for finishing; it's owed. Day eleven.
